«отличник с двойкой по поведению».finding: The phrase appears verbatim in Nikolai Kononov's «Код Дурова» (2012, reprinted 2013) not as the author's own characterisation but as an example of the empty, pre-reporting cliché that used to stand in for Durov's biography: 'Если раньше из его биографии были известны мало что раскрывающие факты («отличник с двойкой по поведению», университетский активист)...'. It rests on the Soviet five-point scale, in which 5 = отлично (an отличник is a straight-5 pupil) and 2 = неудовлетворительно, a fail; under the 1944 rules a 2 for поведение was the most severe grade there was, effectively the paperwork step towards expulsion, with 3 already a formal warning. Numeric conduct marks were replaced in 1970 by примерное / удовлетворительное / неудовлетворительное and abolished outright in 1989, so by Durov's own schooldays (born 1984, School No. 160 then the SPbGU Academic Gymnasium, silver medal) no such grade could literally have been issued: the phrase is a nostalgic set formula, not a record. To a Russian reader in 2013 it reads as an affectionate, slightly worn stock type — the gifted, insolent, teacher-baiting boy whose brains are never in doubt and whose obedience always is — and it sits in a family of scale-based social labels (хорошист с трояками, мир троечников) that sort people by school marks long after school.

rendering.en: a straight-A pupil with a failing grade in conduct

«отличник с двойкой по поведению».rationale: In English I keep connotation and register (the recognisable school-report type: brilliant, ungovernable) and give up the numbers, since 'A' and 'fail' say to an English reader what 5 and 2 say to a Russian one, whereas a literal 'a 2 in conduct' says nothing; the cost is that the neighbouring хорошист/троечник terms lose their shared scale and must be handled by sense ('B-student', 'the world of C-students') rather than by digit. Chinese keeps the same trade, using the standard school term 操行 for the conduct mark so 优等生 / 不及格 carry the contrast natively. Japanese is the one case where the digit survives: the 5段階評価 runs the same direction, so 「2」lands as a near-bottom mark on sight, and 素行だけ preserves the 'everything except behaviour' pivot that the Russian gets from the preposition — what is sacrificed there is the institutional fact that Japanese school reports grade 行動 in words, not numbers, so the figure reads as vivid shorthand rather than as a real entry.

не отливается не то что в граните.term: не отливается не то что в граните
не отливается не то что в граните.finding: The allusion is to Dmitry Medvedev, then president, on 25 December 2009 at a session of the Commission for the Modernisation and Technological Development of the Russian Economy. Sergei Chemezov of Rostekhnologii asked to comment on the president's 'реплика' (remark) about LED lamps not counting as innovation, and Medvedev cut him off: 'Нет, на мою не надо. Моя не реплика уже, а приговор. Реплики у вас. А то, что я говорю, в граните отливается' — 'Mine is no longer a remark, it is a verdict. You have remarks. What I say gets cast in granite.' Two things made it a meme rather than a soundbite: the metaphor is technically wrong (granite is carved, высекают; casting, отливают, is what you do with bronze — engineers said so publicly at the time), and отлить is also crude slang for taking a piss, so the phrase reads as both pompous and accidentally obscene. By 2013 'отлитый в граните' was settled sarcastic shorthand for any self-important official pronouncement — RIA Novosti headlined a 2012 listicle of Medvedev quotes 'Отлитые в граните' — and the setting made it doubly resonant in a Russian tech context, since it was said at the flagship modernisation/Skolkovo commission. The biography's negated form, with 'не то что' as a concessive, says the subject's word does not even reach the granite standard, let alone any firmer one: his pronouncements are provisional, the anti-Medvedev.

rendering.en: not 'cast in granite' — the presidential boast of the day — let alone set in stone
rendering.zh: 别说「铸入花岗岩」（当年梅德韦杰夫的名言），连板上钉钉都算不上
rendering.ja: メドベージェフの言う「花崗岩に鋳込まれる」どころか、石に刻まれることすらない

не отливается не то что в граните.rationale: I kept the literal 'cast in granite' in all three, because the mixed metaphor is just as wrong in English, Chinese and Japanese as in Russian, so the mockery of the pompous malapropism survives translation intact; I then bought back the attribution with a three-word in-text tag, since the sarcasm is unreadable if the reader cannot see a quotation is being thrown back at someone. What I sacrificed is the obscene second layer (отлить as 'take a piss'), which no target language reproduces, and I added the live local idiom — set in stone, 板上钉钉, 石に刻まれる — to carry the 'не то что' concessive that the Russian gets from the negation alone.

Юрий Сапрыкин, публицист, шеф-редактор «.finding: Yuri Gennadyevich Saprykin (b. 1973) is a Russian journalist, music critic and media manager: editor-in-chief of the Moscow city-life and listings magazine Afisha (2003-2008), then its editorial director (2008-2011), briefly editor-in-chief of Slon.ru in 2011, and from 2011 to July 2014 sheff-redaktor (chief/supervising editor) of the merged Rambler-Afisha company, formed when Rambler Internet Holding bought the Afisha company in 2011. To a Russian reader in 2013 his name was not a job title but a marker: Afisha under Saprykin defined the taste of the metropolitan creative class, and he was one of the recognised voices of the 2011-12 Bolotnaya protest wave, so a foreword signed by him placed the Durov book inside liberal, urban, internet-native culture rather than business publishing. 'Публицист' here means a writer of opinion and social commentary (essayist/columnist), not a PR man, and 'Афиша' is a brand name (literally 'playbill/poster') that should not be translated as a common noun. 'Шеф-редактор' is a post above the magazine's own editor-in-chief, covering the merged company's editorial output.

rendering.en: Yuri Saprykin, essayist and chief editor of the merged Rambler-Afisha company (publisher of the Moscow listings magazine Afisha)
rendering.zh: 尤里·萨普雷金，时评作家、兰布勒-阿菲沙（Rambler-Afisha）合并公司总编辑（《阿菲沙》为莫斯科文化生活指南杂志）
rendering.ja: ユーリー・サプルィキン（評論家、統合会社「ランブラー・アフィーシャ」編集主幹。『アフィーシャ』はモスクワの都市文化情報誌）

Юрий Сапрыкин, публицист, шеф-редактор «.rationale: Preserves denotation (the exact post and the brand name kept as a transliterated proper noun, with a short gloss on first mention so a foreign reader sees what Afisha is); sacrifices connotation, since no rendering conveys that Saprykin's byline signals hipster-intelligentsia authority, and drops the Russian distinction between shef-redaktor and glavny redaktor by using 'chief editor' plus 'of the company'.

Мир ловил меня, но не поймал.term: Мир ловил меня, но не поймал
Мир ловил меня, но не поймал.finding: The self-chosen epitaph of Hryhorii Skovoroda (1722-94), the wandering philosopher of the Kyiv-Mohyla tradition, who dug his own grave and asked for these words on the stone; in Ukrainian «Світ ловив мене, та не впіймав», known in Russia in the Russian form the book uses, transmitted via his disciple Kovalensky's biography. For a Russian reader of 2013 it is a schoolbook-famous line, near-proverbial, standing for a man who refused court, church and salary and could not be bought or institutionalised — exactly the frame the author is fitting Durov into. The book does not quote it for its own sake: it inverts it in the very next sentence — «Ботаники поймали мир» ('the nerds caught the world') — so the passage is a chiasmus that only works if the same verb of catching stands in both halves. Note also that Skovoroda is claimed by both Ukrainian and Russian traditions, and calling him simply 'a Russian philosopher' is contested; the book's own wording is neutral, 'философ Григорий Сковорода'.
sources: Кононов Н. В. «Код Дурова» (МИФ, 2013), текст главы: «Мир ловил меня, но не поймал, писал философ Григорий Сковорода. Ботаники поймали мир…»

rendering.en: The world tried to catch me but never caught me
rendering.zh: 世界追捕我，却没有捉住我
rendering.ja: 世は我を捕えんとせしが、捕え得ざりき

Мир ловил меня, но не поймал.rationale: All three keep the denotation and the lapidary tombstone register, and each deliberately re-uses one catching verb (catch / 捉住 / 捕える) so that the author's immediate reversal — 'the nerds caught the world' / 书呆子们捉住了世界 / ナードたちは世界を捕えた — lands as the same word turned around; the Japanese uses classical grammar for epitaph weight, at the cost of easy readability (modern fallback: 「世界は私を捕らえようとしたが、捕らえられなかった」). What is given up is the line's status as a quotation every Russian reader recognises unprompted, so the translator should keep the author's attribution to Skovoroda visible rather than dissolving it into the prose; the common English version 'the world tried to catch me but failed' is more idiomatic but breaks the echo, so it is not used here.

гопники.finding: Гопники (sing. гопник, coll. гопота/гопьё) denotes a specific late-Soviet/post-Soviet class type: young working-class men from the outer housing estates and satellite towns, poorly educated, semi-criminal, moving in territorial courtyard packs, drinking cheap beer or vodka, cracking sunflower seeds, squatting on their heels (the 'на кортах' posture borrowed from prison-yard habit), and dressed in the Adidas/Puma tracksuit that the 1980 Moscow Olympics had made an aspirational item. The word is pejorative and was coined largely by their opposites: неформалы, the Western-music-loving nonconformists whom гопники made a point of hunting and beating in the late 1980s and 1990s (the Lyubertsy crews travelling into Moscow to thrash long-haired kids is the canonical case). So 'bullied the nerds' is not incidental colour but the term's core social content: a gopnik is defined against the bookish, Westward-looking teenager, which is why the word is standard in Russian tech-founder and intelligentsia memoirs. Etymology is contested between гоп-стоп ('mugging', from onomatopoeic гоп 'to jump/hit') and the acronym ГОП, a St Petersburg poorhouse and later 'State Hostel of the Proletariat' whose homeless juvenile residents were the first гопники. For a Russian reader in 2013 the word was still fully live as an insult but already half-retrospective, tagging the 1990s dvor as a period and beginning to acquire the ironic, self-parodic tone that the 'squatting Slav' meme and Hardbass would later globalise.

rendering.en: gopniks — on first mention with a short appositive gloss in the running text, e.g. 'the gopniks, the tracksuited estate toughs', and bare 'gopniks' thereafter
rendering.zh: 首次出现译为「戈普尼克」（gopnik）——穿运动服、住在工人区的街头混混，此后单用「戈普尼克」，需要口语色彩时用「混混」
rendering.ja: 初出は「ゴプニク（ロシア版のヤンキー）」とし、以降は「ゴプニク」。文脈で語調が要る場合は「ジャージ姿のゴプニク」

гопники.rationale: I keep the loanword in all three so the class-and-place specificity survives — gopnik is not a generic hooligan, and any domesticated equivalent (chav, 小混混, ヤンキー alone) would silently relocate the reader — and I buy back the lost transparency with a one-clause gloss at first mention rather than a footnote, so denotation and register are preserved. What I give up is connotation-by-reflex: no target reader feels the contempt-plus-nostalgia the Russian word carries unprompted, and the Japanese ヤンキー gloss in particular trades a little accuracy (no prison-code or nationalist edge) for an instantly legible social type.

вертикали власти.finding: Denotes the top-down chain of executive command Putin began building after May 2000: seven federal districts with presidential plenipotentiaries, a recomposed Federation Council, 'harmonisation' of regional law with federal law, and (after Beslan, 2004) the end of direct gubernatorial elections in favour of presidential nomination. The phrase appeared in Russian media from 1991 and was pushed by Primakov ('vertical of executive power') before Putin made 'ukreplenie vertikali vlasti' — strengthening the power vertical — the slogan of his first term; his July 2000 address to the Federal Assembly demanded 'the single executive power vertical'. Crucially it is the Kremlin's own euphemism: Russian officialdom avoided 'centralisation' because that word is pejorative in political science, so the vertical was the sanctioned, engineering-flavoured way to say it — an image of a streamlined, orderly machine. By 2013 the phrase was worn smooth in Russian press usage and normally carried a resigned or ironic charge: for a reader of a book about a tech founder it means the unaccountable pressure that reaches down from the presidential administration through governors, prosecutors and security services to whoever it wants, and it also names a system widely described as corrupt and hostile to bottom-up initiative. It is a fixed collocation, not a live metaphor; the genitive form here is simply the case the sentence puts it in.
sources: https://ciaotest.cc.columbia.edu/pbei/fiia/0018330/f_0018330_15697.pdf (FIIA Briefing Paper, 'Medvedev's take on the power vertical')
https://politics.rmlt.com.cn/2008/0416/1328.shtml (人民论坛网, on 垂直的权力体系 as the official Russian formulation)
https://src-h.slav.hokudai.ac.jp/publictn/slavic_eurasia_papers/no2/01ueno.pdf (上野俊彦, 'ロシアにおける連邦制改革')
вертикали власти.rationale: All three keep the denotation and the vertical metaphor, which is what makes the term recognisable and what lets a reader link it to standard writing on Putin's Russia; en 'the power vertical' is the settled English form and also reproduces the slightly odd, coined feel of the Russian, while zh 权力垂直体系 and ja 権力の垂直構造 match the wording already used in Chinese and Japanese scholarship on the 2000 federal reforms. What is sacrificed is the connotation and register: the Chinese and Japanese forms read as neutral analytic vocabulary and lose both the Kremlin-euphemism origin and the weary irony a 2013 Russian reader would hear, so if the surrounding sentence depends on that irony it has to be carried by the narration (zh can lean on 中央集权 nearby, ja on 中央集権的な統治機構) rather than by the term itself.

«Сквот ИЕ. Кости в танке», «Наркомпросве.finding: These are two of the magnetic-letter joke nameplates (set in Tahoma, VKontakte's UI font) that hung on the office doors of VKontakte's floors in the Singer House on Nevsky Prospekt, as reported by Nikolai Kononov in 'Код Дурова. Реальная история «ВКонтакте» и ее создателя' (Mann, Ivanov & Ferber, 2013); the same passage lists «Злые пользователи» and «Музей Дурова». They are deliberate nonsense, not descriptive room names: «сквот» is the 1990s-2000s Russian borrowing for a squat — an illegally occupied flat used as an artists'/punk den — so «Сквот ИЕ» casts the Internet Explorer compatibility corner as a squatters' hideout, while «Кости в танке» is an opaque in-house gag with no recoverable referent. «Наркомпросвет» is a fake Soviet acronym built on Наркомпрос (Народный комиссариат просвещения, the People's Commissariat for Enlightenment under Lunacharsky); the padded -свет ending makes it audibly a near-miss on the real abbreviation rather than a quotation of it. To a Russian reader in 2013 the mock-Soviet register was the joke: Kononov frames the whole floor that way, describing the gilded lift as if the programmers had sublet from a fossil ministry and the staff as nerds who had founded their own state, so the plates read as young engineers playing at being a commissariat.

rendering.en: "The IE Squat. Bones in the Tank", "Narkomprosvet"
rendering.zh: 「IE 窝点。坦克里的骨头」、「启蒙人民委员部」
rendering.ja: 「IE 巣窟。戦車の中の骨」「啓蒙人民委員部」

«Сквот ИЕ. Кости в танке», «Наркомпросве.rationale: Rendered literally throughout, preserving denotation and the flat deadpan of an office door plate, and preserving connotation for «Наркомпросвет» by imitating the near-miss rather than translating it: the canonical Chinese and Japanese names for Наркомпрос are 教育人民委员部 / 教育人民委員部, so substituting 启蒙 / 啓蒙 ('enlightenment') gives a reader who knows the institution the same almost-but-not-quite jolt the Russian coinage gives. The cost is that the Soviet echo is inaudible to readers without that background — English keeps the acronym's sound at the price of its sense (an added gloss such as 'People's Commissariat of Enlightenment' can carry the sense if the surrounding text allows it), and «Кости в танке» stays opaque in all three, which is correct, since it is opaque in Russian too. 'Squat' is turned into 窝点 / 巣窟 ('den, hideout') because a bare transliteration would read as the exercise.

генералом этой армии ночи.finding: 'Army of the night' is not a free-standing Russian idiom; it is an imported quotation with two verifiable anchors. First, Norman Mailer's Pulitzer-winning 1968 reportage The Armies of the Night, known in Russian reference works since the Soviet period as «Армии ночи» / «Армия ночи» (Great Soviet Encyclopedia entry on Mailer; ru.wikipedia). Second, and closer to the gloss, the withdrawn 1979 Paramount poster for Walter Hill's The Warriors: 'These are the armies of the night. They are 100,000 strong. They outnumber the cops five to one. They could run New York City.' The film is standard cult viewing in Russia under the title «Воины», and Russian film sites reproduce the poster line in the singular — «Это – армия ночи» — which is exactly the form the biography uses. So a 2013 Russian reader with a VHS-era film memory hears a mock-heroic wink: a leaderless nocturnal multitude, young, numerous, outside official control, that could take the city if it chose. Applied to a technology founder and his following it is affectionate hyperbole, not literal menace; the elevated word 'генерал' over a crowd that has no army is what makes it half-ironic rather than sinister. I could not verify the author's intent directly, only that the collocation circulates in Russian in both these forms.
sources: https://tvfilm.ru/film/c/voinyi-16108/ (Russian rendering of the poster line: «Это – армия ночи»)

rendering.en: the general of this army of the night

генералом этой армии ночи.rationale: All three keep denotation (a leader over a nocturnal horde) and the mock-heroic register that 'general' supplies; what varies is whether the quotation is audible. English is the only one that can carry it for free, since 'army/armies of the night' is the poster wording — if the surrounding sentence tolerates a plural, 'these armies of the night' reproduces it verbatim and is the surer trigger, at the cost of the Russian's singular deixis. Chinese 夜之军团 is the settled form both for Mailer's title and for Chinese renderings of the Warriors tagline, so the allusion is at least recoverable; Japanese has no such handle (the film is known only as 『ウォリアーズ』 and Yurick's novel as 『夜の戦士たち』), so 「夜の軍団」 keeps the image and the irony while giving up the citation, and any need to make the source explicit has to be met with a footnote rather than word choice.

чекисты.finding: Literally 'men of the Cheka' (ВЧК, Dzerzhinsky's 1917 secret police), but in living Russian usage the word covers the whole unbroken line of state-security organs — ЧК, ГПУ/ОГПУ, НКВД, МГБ, КГБ and today's ФСБ/ФСО/СВР — and is what those officers still call themselves (their professional holiday, 20 December, is 'День чекиста'). By 2013 it was ordinary shorthand in the Russian press for the FSB/KGB caste around Putin, who was himself routinely called a чекист; it is double-edged, a badge of honour inside the service and, outside it, a word for the secret-police state with Red Terror and the Gulag behind it. In Kononov's 'Код Дурова' the word appears in a list of folk explanations for VKontakte's rise ('that VKontakte was built by the masons. Or, on the contrary, by the chekists, and Pavel Durov is an invented figure'), i.e. the conspiracy that the network was a security-service project with a front man — a suspicion with real purchase in 2013, when Novaya Gazeta published correspondence showing VK's management handing user data to the FSB and the MVD's Directorate K. The key point for translation is continuity: the Russian word makes the 1917 Cheka and the 2013 FSB one and the same people, and it is spoken, not official.
sources: Николай Кононов, «Код Дурова. Реальная история „ВКонтакте“ и её создателя» (текст: https://testoteka.narod2.ru/raznoe/14.pdf)
чекисты.rationale: In all three I keep the connotation (the security-service caste, spoken about with wary familiarity) and the colloquial register by naming the organ the reader already knows, and give up the denotative Cheka etymology that 'chekists'/契卡分子/チェキスト preserve but that a reader without Russian context cannot decode — 契卡分子 in particular reads as a 1917 historical label, not as living 2013 speech. Where the edition allows a gloss or a translator's note, the calque plus an explanation ('chekists — the security men, from Lenin's Cheka, a name the KGB and FSB never dropped' / 契卡分子（从契卡到克格勃、联邦安全局一脉相承的安全机关人员）/ チェキスト（チェーカー以来のKGB・FSBの治安機関員）) is preferable, since it restores the lineage the short rendering sacrifices.

Vi veri universum vivus vici.finding: A modern (not classical) Latin motto meaning "By the power of truth I, while living, have conquered the universe", built so every word begins with V, hence the initialism V.V.V.V.V. It originates with Aleister Crowley, who took it as his Magister Templi (8=3) motto and signed sections of The Vision and the Voice (1911) V.V.V.V.V.; it is nowhere in Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, the Faust attribution coming via Robert Nye's novel Faust (1980) and then Alan Moore's V for Vendetta, where V credits "a German gentleman named Dr. John Faust". Kononov reports that Durov posted a collage of film stills on his VK page on his birthday in October 2011, captioned "из «Фауста»: Vi veri universum vivus vici – «[Силой] истины я, живущий, покорил вселенную»", seen by 3.6 million subscribers weeks before the December 2011 protests. To a Russian reader in 2013 this read not as erudition but as the V for Vendetta / Guy Fawkes-mask register of that moment — anti-authoritarian defiance with a self-mythologising, faintly messianic edge — and Durov's own "from Faust" tag carries the film's misattribution, which the translation should reproduce rather than silently correct.

rendering.en: Vi veri universum vivus vici — “[By the power] of truth I, living, have conquered the universe”
rendering.zh: Vi veri universum vivus vici——“［凭］真理之力，我，活着的人，征服了宇宙”
rendering.ja: Vi veri universum vivus vici——「真理の［力によって］、生きながら我は宇宙を征服した」

Vi veri universum vivus vici.rationale: The Latin stays untranslated in all three, so denotation and the V-alliteration survive as a visibly foreign motto, and the gloss translates Durov's own bracketed Russian wording — bracketed supplied word and plain literalness included — not the stock English "By the power of truth...". Sacrificed is connotation: no target reader hears the Crowley provenance or the 2011 protest-era charge from the Latin alone, and the wrong "from Faust" attribution is kept.

дом Зингера / Zinger.finding: The building at Nevsky Prospekt 28, on the corner of the Griboyedov Canal directly opposite the Kazan Cathedral: an Art Nouveau block built in 1902–04 by Pavel Suzor as the Russian headquarters of the American Singer sewing-machine company, capped with a glass tower and Amandus Adamson's glass globe because city rules forbade anything taller than the Winter Palace. 'Зингер' is simply how the surname Singer is transliterated into Russian on the German reading, and that form has stuck to the building and to the entities in it (ЗАО «Зингер», which holds the 49-year lease VK bought out in 2023; the Zinger café), which is why Latin-alphabet signage and documents round-trip it back as 'Zinger' rather than 'Singer'. Nationalised in 1919 and, since a bookshop opened there in 1938, known to Petersburgers overwhelmingly as Дом книги, the House of the Book — so calling it 'дом Зингера' is the slightly knowing, insider register. VK rented the seventh floor in 2010 and spread down to the fifth and sixth: for a Russian reader in 2013 the address meant a startup camped in the attic of a federally protected imperial monument above the city's most beloved bookshop, and specifically the window from which Durov and Ilya Perekopsky sailed 5,000-rouble notes on paper aeroplanes into the crowd on City Day, 26 May 2012, filming the scramble.
дом Зингера / Zinger.rationale: In all three I use the name built on the actual firm — Singer, 胜家 (the standard Chinese trade name for Singer machines), シンガー — so the reader gets the denotation and the American-sewing-machine joke for free, and I give up the Russian surface form 'Зингер/Zinger' along with the local shorthand 'Дом книги' that a Petersburger would more often use; where the source text shows the sign, the lease-holding company or the café, keep 'Zinger' / 津格尔 / ジンゲル as a quoted proper name and gloss it once ('the Singer House — Zinger, as the Russians spell it' / 胜家大楼（俄语作“津格尔”，涅瓦大街28号，喀山大教堂对面）/ シンガーハウス（ロシア語では「ジンゲル」、ネフスキー大通り28番地）), and add 'above the House of the Book bookshop' on first mention if the passage relies on the bookshop.
